description_full: Materion Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, produces advanced engineered materials in the United States, Asia, Europe, and internationally. The company operates in four segments: Performance Materials, Electronic Materials, Precision Optics, and Other. It provides beryllium and non-beryllium containing alloy systems and custom engineered metal solutions in strip, bulk, rod, plate, bar, tube, and other customized shapes; engineering and product development services; alloyed metals, beryllium products, and beryllium hydroxide; precision strip, rod, wire, and engineered strip metal products; ToughMet alloys; and SupremEX aluminum silicon carbide metal matrix composite formulation products. The company also operates the bertrandite ore mine and refinery that provides feedstock hydroxide for its beryllium businesses and external sale. In addition, it produces advanced chemicals, microelectronics packaging, precious and non-precious metal, and specialty metal products, including vapor deposition targets, frame lid assemblies, clad and precious metal pre-forms, and high temperature braze materials. Further, the company designs and manufactures precision thin film coatings, optical filters, and assemblies. In addition, it offers inorganic chemicals and powders, specialty coatings, specialty engineered beryllium and copper-based alloys, beryllium composites, ceramics, and engineered clad and plated metal systems. The company sells its products to semiconductor, industrial, aerospace and defense, automotive, energy, consumer electronics, and life sciences through its facilities and service centers, independent distributors and agents, outside distributors, direct sales offices, and independent sales representatives. The company was formerly known as Brush Engineered Materials Inc. and changed its name to Materion Corporation in March 2011. Materion Corporation was founded in 1921 and is based in Mayfield Heights, Ohio.

financial_summary: Materion Corporation is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.9B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $50M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.38× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.6×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (10%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 172% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 36% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 43% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 65% and a beta of 1.20, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.40 vs 5y 1.32), so read it loosely.
About $61.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $23.55 (margin of safety -690%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $12.54 to $40.27 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 38.1 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 18.7 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 77.7 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 41% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $304 on average, 63% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.46).
It runs a 19% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.38x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($13.7M of cash against $481.2M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.6x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.0, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 123 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.6% over 3 years, 8.7% over 5 years and 5.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 22% of profits supports about 1.8% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 8.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.99, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 23%.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (3.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.7%, and institutions hold 100%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $9.4M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (0.2% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 4.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,000 employees, each generates about $596K of revenue, in line with the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $17K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.1M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
